newsitem.title: PANAMA: Cable and Wireless to manage Panama phone system.
newsitem.headline: Cable and Wireless to manage Panama phone system.

text.p: Britain's Cable and Wireless will begin managing Panama's national telephone company INTEL by the end of May or next month, a top company official said Tuesday.

"It will not be much later than the end of May or June. We will work with the government now ... hopefully to conclude the transaction by that time," Geoff Wiggin, managing director of Cable and Wireless West Indies told reporters.
The company won an auction for a 49 percent stake in Panama's National Telecommunications Institute (INTEL) with a bid of $652 million.
"The bid price was the highest paid per capita in the history of telecommunications in Latin America," Finance Minister Miguel Heras said.
"We as Panamanians should feel very grateful and content," he said.
GTE offered $452 million, below the government's base price of $500 million. No other companies had registered to bid in the auction.

One government official expressed surprise with the bid results since GTE had been the only company qualified and in the running for several months last year until Cable and Wireless qualified last December.
"It was a surprise. But their bid (GTE) was too low," the official said.
Heras said GTE's bid was based on a $400 million reference price suggested by Salomon Brothers, the government's adviser on the sale.

Wiggins said the Cable and Wireless bid was based "on the ... possibilities we saw for services in Panama. We see synergies with other operations in Hong Kong and Singapore, and the proximity of the Caribbean," he said.
Cable and Wireless remains one of the few major international telecoms players that can boast access to lucrative Asian markets via its majority stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd .

Cable and Wireless is the third largest carrier of international traffic and operates the world's largest cableship fleet. Cable and Wireless West Indies represents 22 businesses in the Caribbean region, he said.
"We have a capital program that will require us to spend a lot of money in Panama in order to upgrade the systems and bring new services and products to the customers," said Wiggin.
"The exact investment program I'm not prepared to talk about just right now," he said.
Government officials have said they expect INTEL's new operator to invest at least $500 million. Line density is expected to increase from 12.2 per 100 inhabitants to about 25 per 100 inhabitants.
The concession also requires Cable and Wireless to set up a Band B cellular service within 12 months.
A consortium led by BellSouth Corp won the license to set up and operate Panama's first cellular network, Band A, with a $72.6 million bid last year.
